articles.title: DH Impact | Attempt to convert 1,096 acres of Sandur forest to revenue land nixed
articles.summary: Bengaluru: Three months after DH revealed that 1,096 acres of forest in Ballari’s Sandur was stripped of legal protection through an illegal mutation, revenue authorities have restored the status of ‘forest’ for the land days ahead of a hearing in the National Green Tribunal (NGT) . In a notification dated April 1, 1890 the Madras Presidency had declared as forest the land in survey numbers 165/A, 165/B, 177/c and 1/B of Somalapur village, Choranur hobli, Sandur. In January 2024, the then assistant commissioner issued an order changing the status of the four survey numbers from forest to ‘kharab’ (waste/revenue) land. While the exercise was carried out to ostensibly fix errors in revenue documents, a senior forest officer told DH that the (ex parte) order was issued without seeking the department’s opinion. Karnataka: Protected for 134 years, 1,096 acres of Sandur forest converted into revenue land Under the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 and its amendment, Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, no forest can be converted into non-forest land or used for any non-forest purposes without the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change clearance. The National Green Tribunal’s (NGT) principal bench had registered a suo motu case based on the DH report. On September 8, the NGT ordered notice to the head of the state forest department, the Director General, MoEF&CC and others. Sources in Sandur said two private mining companies had eyed the land. Reacting to the DH report, unnamed revenue officials had tried to portray the changes in the document as “technical problems” and not deliberate land conversion. However, in a report submitted to the assistant commissioner of Ballari, a copy of which is with DH , the tahsildar of Sandur taluk had acknowledged that the Record of Rights, Tenancy and Crops (RTC) for four survey numbers reflect the change in the status as ‘B-Kharab land’. Attaching a report from the revenue inspector of Choranur, tahsildar Anil Kumar endorsed that the land parcels be mutated in favour of the forest department. DH verified the latest RTCs, which now bear the name of ‘Somalapuram Reserved Forest’ in Column 9 (owner) and explain the rights by pointing to the Fort St George Gezette Notification No 148 Dated 01/04/1890. The changes have been made as per the orders of the assistant commissioner. Activist Dinesh Kallahalli, who obtained documents under RTI to show the illegal mutation, said the government must order an inquiry. “How is it possible to change the century-old forest into revenue land? There was the illegal pipeline built to enable land grabbing. All these need to be investigated,” he said. Ballari DCF Basavaraj K N could not be reached for a comment.

articles.title: Five new frog species discovered in Arunachal Pradesh
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered five new frog species in the forests of Arunachal Pradesh, including India’s first documented snail-eating frog, highlighting the rich biodiversity of the Eastern Himalayas. The new species belong to the genus Jingophrys, commonly known as Diminutive Horned Frogs, and were identified following five years of field exploration by researchers from Delhi University and Harvard University. The genus is characterised by prominent, horn-like skin structures around the upper eyelids. Three species have been named after local communities, geography and language. The Tanii Horned Frog (Jingophrys taniitatii) is named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, which inhabits the Ziro Valley and speaks Apatani. Its scientific name combines ‘tanii’, referring to the community, with ‘tatii’, the Apatani word for frogs and toads. The Siang Horned Frog (Jingophrys siangensis) is named after the Siang region. A silent monsoon for the Western Ghats’ frogs The third species, Jingophrys tanogogo, gets its name from the Apatani word for snails. Researchers discovered whole land snail shells inside its gut using 3D micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) imaging. This is the first documented record of snail-eating behaviour in a frog in India and the first published report of such behaviour in the family Megophryidae, which is widely distributed across Asia. Researchers also found snail shells in the stomach contents of another species, the previously known Jingophrys vegrandis. “It is surprising that these frogs can ingest complete snail shells much larger than their heads, raising further questions about the feeding mechanisms that enable such behaviour,” said S.D. Biju, senior professor at Delhi University and a member of the research team. The five new species increase the known diversity of Jingophrys in India seven-fold. The study also records two species previously known from China for the first time in India. DNA-based analyses reveal distinct evolutionary lineages and rapid diversification of horned frogs in the Eastern Himalayas. Researchers suggest these patterns may be linked to geological and climatic changes over millions of years, including Himalayan uplift and the development of the South Asian monsoon. The findings reinforce the Eastern Himalayas’ status as a critical amphibian hotspot, with significant undocumented biodiversity requiring further research and conservation. “Arunachal Pradesh is a truly understudied region of India hiding rich and endemic frog fauna. Some of the new species are extremely secretive and found in remote forests only during a short breeding season,” Biju added. The study, led by Sonali Garg of Harvard University’s Museum of Comparative Zoology, was recently published in Royal Society Open Science

articles.title: Nepal’s climate pitch for the world: A call for climate disaster funding
articles.summary: After the devastating glacier collapse that killed more than 1,500, Nepal arrived at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey looking for help. What it found was a system that many say is ill-equipped to help vulnerable countries recover from climate disasters. The catastrophe in August occurred after a wall of rock and ice crumbled, triggering a flood that wiped out towns and left thousands missing. Nepal says it will cost roughly $5 billion to rebuild. But so far, Nepal has received pledges for less than 10% of that amount, with much of it in the form of loans. The devastation in Nepal has become a crucial test case for whether the global community can deliver quick financial relief when disasters strike. Many at the talks, including Nepal and small island nations whose low-lying countries face repeated typhoons and storm damage, said getting help to rebuild could take months or even years, a delay they can’t afford. UN climate loss and damage fund sets aside $20 million for Nepal floods “Our melting mountains cannot wait for our negotiations to catch up with their changing reality,” Shisir Khanal, the Nepali foreign minister, told leaders at the climate summit, known as COP31. This week, an effort by Nepal and Bhutan to make glacial ice melt and other issues facing mountain communities a formal part of the climate negotiations stalled. At the same time, a fund created to help vulnerable countries cope with the economic consequences of climate disasters has promised Nepal just $21.6 million, a fraction of its need. “We are suffering from a disaster which we did not cause,” said Pramesh Pokharel, a Nepali activist who works with small-scale farmers. “Most greenhouse gas emissions are caused by the Global North, rich people and multinational corporations.” Developed nations and rich companies should foot the bill for Nepal’s recovery, Pokharel said. “It’s about who bears the cost of the loss and damages, and who should pay,” he said. “We are demanding that those who are polluting, they must pay the cost of the devastation we are facing.” In the months since the disaster, Nepal has received patchwork pledges from around the globe. The World Bank said it would make $170 million in emergency financing available. The United States initially offered $500,000 in aid, then expanded that sum to $36 million after Jensen Huang, the former CEO of Nvidia, pledged $10 million. A handful of countries, including Australia and Japan, pledged a combined $40 million. The United Nations helped raise an additional $50 million. The four entities that have historically provided Nepal with the most support are India, China, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank. All those pledges still fall short. Assessments conducted in the days after the catastrophe concluded that damages totalled about $1.8 billion. Rebuilding the devastated areas with improved infrastructure, the government concluded, would cost roughly $5 billion, equivalent to about 10% of Nepal’s gross domestic product. After the Aug. 26 glacier collapse, the Loss and Damage Fund, created in 2024 under the UN climate treaty framework to help nations recover from climate-fueled disasters, held a special meeting to allow Nepal to submit a fast-track aid proposal, which led to the $21.6 million commitment. “When Nepal happened, there was a lot of pressure from all of us,” said Ibrahima Cheikh Diong, executive director of the Loss and Damage Fund. “This is why the fund was set up. Even though we’re not sitting on billions of dollars, our board couldn’t afford to just do nothing.” Nepal’s finance minister, Swarnim Waglé, said his country’s need remained enormous. “When the need is $5 billion, $20 million is nothing,” Waglé said. “However, this is acknowledging that very poor countries, the low-income countries in the fragile Himalayas, are bearing the brunt of the Western industrialisation.” This week, Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah is in India seeking a $2 billion package of credits, loans and grants. Nepal was also looking to China to help rebuild its physical infrastructure destroyed by the flood, including the main trading corridor between the two countries, Waglé said. It was also seeking below-market-rate loans and grants from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, he said. “I request the U.S. to step up,” Waglé said. “We’re in this together, and cooperation demands that we have to help countries in need.” After Tibet-Nepal flash floods, BRICS agrees on early warning data integration, disaster resilience The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Nepal has called the glacier collapse a climate disaster. World Weather Attribution, a scientific group, said human-caused climate change made the conditions that led to the collapse more likely. “The permafrost thawing and the glaciers melting, that’s a direct cause of global warming,” Waglé said. “Because of global warming, ice is retreating, glaciers are melting, and this rock got exposed to the elements, and that accentuated the vulnerability.” The disaster in Nepal has forced leaders from other developing nations to find new ways of seeking assistance. This week, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori appealed directly to Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for aid to help cope with the effects of El Niño. She walked away with a pledge of $22.5 million. Pacific island nations have started an endowment fund to help disaster-proof their countries and “cut out the red tape,” President Surangel Whipps Jr. of Palau said. The fund, known as the Pacific Resilience Facility, aims to raise $1.5 billion, a reference to the 1.5-degree target in the 2015 Paris climate agreement that experts now say will not be met.

articles.title: India’s fugitive tycoons: Wanted at home, welcome abroad
articles.summary: In November 2005, Portugal put Abu Salem on a plane to Mumbai. Lisbon had few doubts. India wanted him for the 1993 Bombay blasts, which killed more than 250 people. Portugal sought only two guarantees: that he would not be hanged and that he would not serve more than 25 years. India gave its word. In 2022, the Supreme Court held the government to that promise. From arrest to handover took three years. By the standards of extradition, that is almost brisk. Twelve years later, in June 2017, Vijay Mallya sat in the stands at The Oval in London and watched India play cricket. He had left the year before, owing the banks around Rs 9,000 crore. India’s formal request for his extradition had been made four months earlier. He lost his appeals in the English courts by 2020. He is still in England. Nine cricket seasons have come and gone. Why does the bomber return home in three years, while the businessman can still enjoy cricket in England? These two scenes explain the numbers better than any white paper. Between 2019 and July 2026, India brought back 274 fugitives from 36 countries. Only nine faced fraud or financial charges. The remaining fugitives were wanted on charges such as murder, sexual offences, organised crime, terrorism and drug trafficking. Is the easy reading – that our diplomats and law-enforcement agencies fail when the man is rich – really the better one? Or does the world simply agree on some crimes and not on others? Murder is murder in Lisbon and in Lucknow. A bomb in a crowded market horrifies every jurisdiction. No country wants a killer living down the street. When India asks for one, the host state is usually relieved to see him go. It will demand assurances on the death penalty and prison conditions, then hand him over. A financial crime carries no such moral weight. It exists because a statute says it does. Extradition treaties reflect this through dual criminality: the alleged conduct itself must be an offence in both countries. Courts look past the label and ask whether the same acts would be criminal under their own law. A wilful default, a breach of foreign-exchange rules, or a money-laundering charge resting on an Indian predicate offence may find no counterpart abroad. What Delhi calls fraud, London may call a failed business. Nirav Modi’s counsel described the PNB affair as “ill-advised lending”. Mallya’s team said Kingfisher was an airline that went bust, as airlines do. Is a balance-sheet failure the same offence as a bomb in a market? Most foreign courts answer no. The big cases cleared that first hurdle. English magistrates found a case for Mallya and Nirav Modi to answer. Belgian judges accepted six of the seven charges against Mehul Choksi. But clearing dual criminality only opens the next gates. The foreign court asks whether the prison is safe and whether the trial will be fair. It also examines whether the prosecution has political motives. A person accused of violent crimes loses sympathy at each gate. A non-violent one does not. He arrives in a suit, with a medical file and the best barristers money can buy. In February 2025, the English High Court refused to send the arms dealer Sanjay Bhandari to India. It feared for his safety in Tihar. Every lawyer in London trying to shield a fugitive from extradition has read that judgment. How many more such judgments must we collect before we notice the pattern? Now consider how the host country sees him. For years Britain sold residence to the wealthy through its investor visa. It closed that scheme only in 2022. Antigua sold Choksi its citizenship in 2017. Belgium hosted him as a resident whose wife is a Belgian national. Lalit Modi has acquired a British passport. One country’s economic offender becomes another country’s entrepreneur, or refugee, or its favoured guest. A man who brings capital is welcome. A man who brings a gun is not. Is that hypocrisy peculiar to the West? Or is it simply how states have always behaved? Our own politics make the problem worse. When ministers and rival parties turn a fugitive into a campaign slogan, they hand his lawyers a gift. Political persecution is a defence in every extradition treaty. The louder the speeches in Delhi, the stronger the affidavit in London. Does a fugitive gain more from Indian TV channels than from any loophole in the law? SANJAY HEGDE India should also look in the mirror. Sheikh Hasina has lived in Delhi since August 2024. A Bangladeshi tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia last November. Dhaka wants her back. New Delhi has not sent her, citing treaty safeguards, as other countries do when dealing with India. To Dhaka, she is a convict. To Delhi, she is a guest whose life may be in danger. This is not to make a judgment on her case but to underscore that the principle of sovereign discretion cuts both ways. If every sovereign keeps the right to decide whom it shelters, why should the same right not be exercised against India? What, then, should India do? First, accept that the world will never treat a defaulter like a terrorist. Will shouting change that? Second, fix what foreign judges examine. They read reports on our prisons. They count the years our undertrials wait. A country where trials drag on for a decade gives every fugitive his best argument. Our assurances work only if our courts can enforce them. The Abu Salem judgment showed that they can. Third, follow the money rather than the man. The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act lets India confiscate assets. The government says it has recovered over Rs 14,000 crore from Mallya’s assets alone. For the banks, is recovering the money more important than bringing him back to face justice? Diplomacy has its place. Foreign secretaries can press their counterparts, and prime ministers can raise names at summits. But extradition is a legal process conducted in foreign courts, under foreign law, by judges who owe us nothing. They will send back the bomber without much fuss. They will think long and hard about the businessman. Abu Salem sits in Taloja jail. Mallya watches cricket in England. Does this reflect a failure of nerve in South Block, or simply how the world ranks crimes? India can grumble about that ranking, or it can make its courts and prisons a place a foreign judge would trust. (The writer is a senior advocate designated by the Supreme Court)
